title: The Little Trick Hiding in a Bar of Soap
blurb: Water cannot wash grease away on its own. Soap is the go-between that makes it happen, and people have been boiling it from fat and ashes for four thousand years.

blocks.prompt: The Little Trick Hiding in a Bar of Soap
blocks.text: Water is good at washing off mud. Water is not good at washing off grease. Grease and water do not mix. Pour cooking oil into a cup of water and watch. The oil floats on top in a shiny puddle. It will not blend in, no matter how long you wait. Soap fixes this. Every tiny bit of soap has two ends. One end holds on to water. The other end holds on to grease. When you rub soap on your hands, the soap grabs the grease and the water grabs the soap. Then it all goes down the drain together. Soap is the middle piece that makes the two sides hold hands.

blocks.prompt: Why Grease Runs From Water
blocks.text: Picture this. You wash a muddy hand under the tap and the mud gives up right away. You wash a greasy hand the same way and the grease just sits there, shining. The water runs straight over it. Here is why. Water sticks to water. Grease sticks to grease. Neither one wants anything to do with the other. That is why cooking oil floats in a shiny puddle on top of a glass of water instead of mixing in. Soap solves the problem by cheating. A soap molecule is shaped a bit like a tiny tadpole. The head end loves water and holds on tight. The long tail end hates water, so it buries itself in grease instead. When soap meets a greasy hand, thousands of tails dig into the grease while thousands of heads stay out in the water. The soap wraps each drop of grease in a little ball, with all the water loving heads facing outward. Now the water has something to grab. The whole ball rinses down the drain. Soap does not kill the grease. It just gives the water a handle.

blocks.prompt: The Molecule With Two Minds
blocks.text: Soap is older than glass, older than paper, and older than most countries. Clay tablets from Babylon, made around 2800 BCE, carry a recipe for boiling fat together with ashes. Nobody in Babylon knew any chemistry. They had simply noticed that this particular mixture lifted dirt out of cloth, and they decided the recipe was worth writing down. What they had stumbled onto is called saponification. Wood ash soaked in water makes a harsh, slippery liquid called an alkali. Boil that liquid together with animal fat or plant oil and the fat molecules come apart and rearrange themselves. What is left behind, once it cools and hardens, is soap. A soap molecule is a strange piece of engineering. One end carries an electric charge, and water pulls it close. The other end is a long chain of carbon and hydrogen, and water pushes it away. Chemists call a molecule built like this a surfactant, and its two ends spend their whole existence in disagreement. That disagreement is the useful part. Drop soap into greasy water and the molecules arrange themselves into hollow balls called micelles. Every tail tucks inward, gripping the grease. Every charged head faces outward into the water. Each speck of grease ends up packed inside its own soap ball, and the water carries the whole cargo away without ever touching the grease at all. So soap is not really a cleaner in the way most people picture one. It is a translator. It lets two substances that refuse to speak to each other pass something between them.

blocks.prompt: The Cheapest Medicine Ever Invented
blocks.text: In 1847 a doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis noticed a pattern in a Vienna hospital that nobody could explain. The maternity ward run by doctors was losing women to fever at several times the rate of the ward run by midwives. Same building. Same city. Same illness. The difference, Semmelweis eventually worked out, was that the doctors arrived on the ward straight from performing autopsies, and the midwives did not. He ordered his staff to scrub their hands in a chlorine solution before touching a patient. The death rate collapsed. He had no idea why it worked. Germs had not been discovered yet. Semmelweis had evidence and no explanation, and his colleagues found the suggestion insulting. A gentleman's hands, they insisted, were clean. He was pushed out of the profession and died in an asylum in 1865, years before Louis Pasteur and Joseph Lister finally made his numbers make sense. The chemistry underneath his discovery is almost embarrassingly simple. A soap molecule has two ends that want opposite things: a charged head that water pulls toward itself, and an oily tail that water shoves away. Soap also does something water cannot manage alone. Water molecules cling so hard to one another that water beads up instead of spreading out, a force called surface tension. Soap wedges itself between those clinging molecules and loosens their grip, so water can finally soak into the fabric or the skin instead of rolling off it. Then comes the part that matters most. Many of the viruses that make people sick, including influenza and the coronaviruses, wrap themselves in a coat of fat. That coat is what holds the virus together. Soap's oily tails slide into the fatty coat, pry it apart, and the virus falls into pieces. This is why the advice is to scrub for twenty seconds rather than rinse for two. You are not chasing germs off your skin. You are taking them apart. Semmelweis was right for reasons he could not name, and it cost him everything. The cheapest life saving technology on Earth is fat boiled with ashes, and people once had to be argued into using it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Fats are triglycerides: three fatty acid chains on a glycerol backbone
Saponification splits them with a strong alkali
Amphiphile: from the Greek for loving both
Water's cohesion comes from hydrogen bonds
Hard water turns soap into insoluble scum
Detergents were designed to beat hard water

blocks.prompt: Loving Both: How a Bar of Soap Actually Works
blocks.text: Almost everything soap does follows from a single fact: a soap molecule cannot decide what it wants to be. Start with how it is made. Fats and oils, whether pressed from an olive or rendered from an animal, are triglycerides, meaning three long fatty acid chains hitched to a small glycerol backbone. Soak wood ash in water and you get a strongly alkaline solution. Boil the two together and the alkali snaps those chains off the backbone, leaving glycerol on one side and, on the other, the salts of the fatty acids. Those salts are soap. The reaction is called saponification, and it has not changed in four thousand years. Clay tablets from Babylon dated to roughly 2800 BCE record fat boiled with ashes. Pliny the Elder, writing in the first century, described a substance the Gauls made from tallow and ash and called sapo, though the Romans of his day mostly used it on their hair rather than their skin. Now look closely at what saponification produces. Each soap molecule is a long hydrocarbon tail with an electrically charged carboxylate head bolted onto one end. The head is polar, and water welcomes it. The tail is nonpolar, and water rejects it absolutely. A molecule carrying both properties at once is called an amphiphile, from the Greek for loving both, and that permanent internal conflict is the entire engine of cleaning. Water alone fails at grease for a reason worth stating precisely. Water molecules are polar, so they cling to one another through hydrogen bonds. This cohesion is why water beads on a leaf, and why the surface of a pond forms a skin strong enough to hold up an insect. It is also why water cannot wet an oily surface: the water would rather hold on to itself than spread across something nonpolar. Soap breaks the deadlock twice over. First, its molecules crowd into the water's surface with their tails sticking out, which weakens the hydrogen bonding there and drops the surface tension, so water can finally spread and soak in. Second, out in the body of the water, soap molecules assemble themselves into micelles: hollow spheres with every tail tucked inside and every charged head facing out. Grease gets trapped in the oily interior. The exterior is charged and water friendly, so it rinses away without argument, cargo included. The same geometry explains the medical story. Many viruses, including influenza and the coronaviruses, are packaged inside an envelope built from lipids, and that envelope is what holds them together. Soap's tails are indifferent to what kind of oil they burrow into, so they slide straight into the envelope and pull it apart. The virus does not run away. It comes undone. Twenty seconds of scrubbing is not superstition. It is roughly how long the mechanical work takes. Soap has one real weakness. In hard water, dissolved calcium and magnesium ions latch onto the carboxylate heads and form an insoluble curd, the gray ring left around a bathtub. Every molecule that ends up in that ring is a molecule no longer cleaning anything. Twentieth century chemists answered by designing synthetic detergents with heads that hard water ions cannot precipitate, which is why the bottle at your kitchen sink is almost certainly not soap at all. Which leaves a strange fact to sit with. The most effective public health measure in human history is not a machine or a drug. It is fat, boiled with ashes, invented by people who could not have explained a single step of what they were doing, and understood properly only thousands of years after it had already started saving lives.
